PMGT1852 Week 05

PMGT1852 Week 5 - Preparing a Facilitated Session

The five Ps of preparation

A facilitated session is a meeting in which a facilitator guides a group through a process to achieve an agreed outcome. Preparation begins with the outcome, not with a detailed agenda.

Element

Meaning

Main preparation question

Purpose

The reason for meeting and the overall objective

Why are we meeting?

Product

The outcomes that demonstrate achievement of the purpose

What should exist or change by the end?

Participants

The people needed to contribute knowledge, make decisions or implement results

Who needs to take part?

Probable Issues

Matters that must be addressed or could disrupt progress

What issues should we anticipate?

Process

The sequence of activities used to achieve the outcomes

How will the group do the work?

Use the sequence Purpose -> Product -> Participants -> Probable Issues -> Process. Design the process last because it must serve the other four elements. Starting with speakers or an agenda can lock the meeting into activities that do not deliver its actual purpose.

Defining products with the three Hs

A product need not be a physical document. The three Hs distinguish tangible, intellectual and relational outcomes.

Dimension

Meaning

Examples of the kind of outcome sought

Hands

Tangible deliverables and practical outputs

An agreed statement, a prioritised list or an action plan

Heads

Knowledge and understanding

A shared understanding of the problem or the available options

Hearts

Beliefs, attitudes, trust and commitment

Confidence in the process and commitment to implementing its result

An agenda may produce a document without achieving understanding or commitment. Considering all three dimensions makes the intended result more complete.

Selecting and briefing participants

Choose people who understand the issue, have a stake in the outcome, can decide or advise, are respected opinion leaders, or are open to considering alternatives. A stakeholder is a person or group that can affect or be affected by the work.

The participant mix should cover different communication styles, knowledge and experience, departments or stakeholder groups, and organisational levels. Diversity of perspective is useful only if the process lets those perspectives be heard.

Indicative session sizes

Meeting type

Main purpose

Suggested number of participants

Resolution

Resolve an issue or reach agreement

3-9

Creation

Generate ideas or develop something new

7-16

Direction-setting

Establish a shared direction

12-24

Review

Examine information, progress or results

2-100+

These ranges guide process design; they do not guarantee adequate representation or quality of evidence.

Before the meeting, explain the purpose, products and proposed process. Ask participants about their concerns, whether the process is suitable and what could improve it. Explain practical arrangements and request early arrival.

Anticipating probable issues

Category

Definition

Preparation response

Topics

Issues that must be discussed to achieve the purpose

Include them explicitly in the process

Ditches

Difficult issues that could derail the meeting

Anticipate sensitivities and plan how to address them

Red herrings

Irrelevant issues that distract from the purpose

Recognise the diversion and guide discussion back to the task

A difficult issue is not automatically irrelevant. Labelling a genuine concern a red herring can prevent the group from dealing with an important barrier.

Designing the process and meeting notice

Once the other four Ps are clear, select activities and order them into an agenda. Each activity should contribute to an expected product.

Ideally, send a meeting notice at least one week in advance. Include:

• Purpose and expected products.

• Proposed agenda.

• Location and practical arrangements.

• Gathering time, followed by the formal starting and ending times.

• Participants.

• Materials, advance reading and preparation tasks.

Set the gathering time before the formal start so arrival and settling in do not consume the working session.

Sponsor management

The sponsor is usually the person requesting the meeting or the person responsible for achieving its purpose and products. Discuss the five Ps, the meaning of success, expected outcomes, concerns, participation and practical arrangements with the sponsor.

Sponsor attendance has benefits and risks:

Benefits

Risks

Demonstrates support

Can inhibit candid contributions

Provides history and context

Can reduce creativity or encourage dominance

Supports implementation

Can weaken the group's ownership of results

Attendance is especially useful when the sponsor is a key implementer, the meeting is strategic, background knowledge is important or implementation support is needed. Limit participation when the sponsor is primarily an approver or their presence is likely to inhibit discussion.

Ask the sponsor not to be the first, second or third person to speak on an issue. Hearing other participants first reduces the risk that their comments merely follow the sponsor's position.

Preparation checklist

Interview the sponsor.

Identify the purpose, outcomes, participants and barriers.

Draft the objective statement and agenda.

Prepare a sample deliverable so the required output is concrete.

Tailor the facilitation process to the group and task.

Allocate responsibility for practical arrangements and documentation.

Brief the facilitation team and communicate with participants.

Learn enough about the business area to understand the discussion.

Prepare materials and arrange the meeting space.

Prepare the opening statement.

Preparation can require as much time as, or more time than, running the session.

Cases and applications

Principals' Conference

A detailed agenda and speakers were selected before agreement on the purpose and outcomes. Different groups subsequently wrote different purpose statements, and nearly half the agenda had to be redesigned. The case demonstrates why agreement on purpose and products must precede detailed process planning.

Vision Councils

The case highlights the substantial time needed for preparation and the risk of unresolved disagreement between sponsor and facilitator. Agreement on outcomes and process is part of preparation, not something to assume once the meeting begins.

Task force

A task force is a group formed to address a defined issue. The sponsor commonly provides information for the first four Ps. The facilitator and task-force members then determine the process appropriate to that work.

Town Hall 2050

In a workshop facilitated by John, discussion moved from a design focus into an argument about gender. The preparation issue is whether likely concerns and potential diversions had been anticipated. A useful response is to identify probable issues, agree discussion rules, prepare neutral redirection wording and communicate the meeting's purpose beforehand. A concern should still be assessed for relevance before being treated as a diversion.

For a Sydney local character statement, meaning a statement describing the distinctive qualities a community wants its place to express, the three Hs can guide question design:

• Hands: "What concrete features should the local character statement describe?"

• Heads: "What should participants understand about the area's distinctive character by the end?"

• Hearts: "What would help participants trust and support the statement?"

These questions illustrate how to distinguish outputs, understanding and commitment; they are not claims about what workshop participants actually said.
